newsitem.title: USA: San Francisco mayor unveils stadium financial plan.
newsitem.headline: San Francisco mayor unveils stadium financial plan.

text.p: San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown unveiled a financial plan Tuesday that he said would guarantee the city would never have to dip into its general fund to pay off bonds for a proposed stadium-mall complex.

Brown said Morgan Stanley Group Inc would underwrite the bonds, and Financial Security Assurance, a unit of Financial Security Assurance Holdings Ltd, would issue municipal bond insurance to guarantee their repayment.
Under the proposed financing, San Francisco would not be obligated to make payments from its general fund in excess of the revenues generated from the stadium project, Brown said.
Brown told a news conference his plan would ensure "that on any day that revenue stream is not adequate to pay back the due amount, the insurance company will pick up the tab."

San Francisco residents will vote June 3 on the $100 million lease revenue bond measure. The bond funds would help to finance the city's share of the proposed $525 million San Francisco 49ers football stadium and shopping complex.
The bond measure has, however, made little headway with voters. The proposal trails by nine percentage points according to a San Francisco Chronicle poll published Tuesday.
Mayor Brown said he hoped his financial plan would persuade stadium critics to support the stadium bond measure on June 3. "I have done the best deal the city can get," Brown told reporters.
Morgan Stanley said it would structure the bond deal to protect the city's general fund if tax and lease revenues generated by the project fell below projections.
"We believe this is a very good credit and inherently doable," Morgan Stanley principal Robert Larkins said. "This is a good deal for the city."

FSA Managing Director Suzanne Finnegan said FSA reviewed the legal, credit and financial components of the proposed bond deal and was "confident that the proposed lease revenue bond financing can be structured with FSA insurance."
Stadium opponents said bond proposal was still too risky for the city, despite the mayor's financial plan.
"The city of San Francisco is still on the line for hundreds of millions of dollars for infrastructure costs and city services," said Jim Ross, who heads the campaign opposed to the project.
